Food_Recommender/shared_functions.py.purpose: The retrieval engine for a food search demo: load a JSON food catalogue, repair missing fields, embed every dish into ChromaDB, then answer free-text queries - including intent words like "lowest calories" or "under 300 calories" that pure vector search cannot handle.
Food_Recommender/shared_functions.py.run: python interactive_search.py   (this module is imported, not run directly)

sections.title: Module docstring - the whole pipeline on one page
sections.start: """Shared retrieval helpers for the Food Recommender demo.
sections.why: Before reading a single function, the docstring gives you the five stages and the design decisions. This is what good module documentation looks like.

sections.title: Imports and the shared in-memory client
sections.why: One client object is shared by every collection this module creates, so there is exactly one place that decides whether data is in RAM or on disk.

sections.title: Stage 1 - load_food_data(): repair every record
sections.why: Hand-written JSON is never perfectly uniform. This function fixes each record up front so no other function needs defensive checks.

sections.title: Stage 2a - choosing the ChromaDB configuration shape
sections.why: ChromaDB changed the type of one argument between 0.6.x and 1.x. This helper tries the modern shape and falls back - a compatibility shim you should understand before editing.

sections.title: Stage 2b - create_similarity_search_collection()
sections.why: Deletes any old collection and builds a fresh one with cosine distance and the MiniLM embedding function bound to it.

sections.title: Stage 3 - populate_similarity_collection(): flatten, embed, insert
sections.why: Every dish becomes one rich sentence for embedding plus a flat metadata dictionary for filtering and display.

sections.title: Stage 4a - perform_similarity_search()
sections.start: def perform_similarity_search(collection, query: str, n_results: int = 5) -> List[Dict]:
sections.why: The pure semantic search: embed the query, take the nearest five, convert distance into a similarity score.

sections.title: Stage 4b - perform_filtered_similarity_search()
sections.start: def perform_filtered_similarity_search(collection, query: str, cuisine_filter: str = None,
sections.why: Same ranking, but the candidate set is restricted inside the database using metadata - cuisine equality and a calorie ceiling.

sections.title: Stage 5a - the typo table and three calorie regexes
sections.why: Small, explicit, testable rules instead of an LLM call. Cheap, fast and predictable - the right tool for a demo.

sections.title: Stage 5b - _known_cuisines()
sections.why: Reads the real cuisine values out of the database so the parser never hard-codes a list that drifts from the JSON file.

sections.title: Stage 5c - parse_search_constraints()
sections.why: Turns "deserts with lowest calroes" into four fields: fixed typo, calorie cap, sort flag and cuisine filter.

sections.title: Stage 5d - perform_calorie_aware_search()
sections.start: def perform_calorie_aware_search(collection, query: str, n_results: int = 5,
sections.why: The function the CLI actually calls. Relevance first, numbers second: build a semantic candidate pool, then re-rank by calories.

notes.title: The pipeline diagram in text
notes.text: Load, create collection, populate, search, return ranked dictionaries. Read this ASCII diagram as the table of contents: every function below is one arrow.

notes.title: Why almost nothing raises
notes.text: Every public helper catches its own errors and returns an empty list. The CLI can therefore loop forever without a `try` around every call. The trade-off: a real bug can look like "no results found", so watch the printed error messages.

notes.title: The bug that looks like bad maths
notes.text: On chromadb 0.6.x the configuration object only records the metric; the local index reads `hnsw:space` from the collection metadata. Set it in one place only and you silently get squared L2, so `1 - distance` can go negative. This note is the reason the code below sets both.

notes.title: One ephemeral client
notes.text: In-memory again: every run rebuilds the index from the JSON file. That makes demos reproducible, but it also means the collection must be populated before any query - a fact the CLI's `main()` follows strictly.

notes.title: Always state the encoding
notes.text: `encoding='utf-8'` prevents mojibake on Windows for accented dish names. Without it Python uses the platform default, which is not UTF-8 on every machine.

notes.title: Numbers become strings
notes.text: The JSON stores `food_id` as an integer; ChromaDB needs string ids. Converting here means `populate_similarity_collection` never has to think about types - one normalisation point, many happy consumers.

notes.title: Inert defaults instead of crashes
notes.text: Missing fields get safe values: 0 calories, empty description, `Unknown` cuisine. Note that `food_name` is deliberately **not** defaulted - a nameless dish cannot be shown to a user, and ChromaDB metadata rejects `None`.

notes.title: Nesting becomes a sentence
notes.text: `food_features` is a dictionary per dish (`taste`, `texture`, `appearance`...). Flattening it into `"sweet, crisp and tender, golden brown"` gives the embedding builder one predictable string instead of a dict whose keys differ per dish.

notes.title: Return [] rather than raise
notes.text: A missing or broken JSON file results in an empty list and a printed reason. The caller prints "Loaded 0 food items", which is far more debuggable than a traceback for a beginner.

notes.title: Why the *Internal* classes
notes.text: ChromaDB serialises configuration objects with a `_type` field. Building the public Interface classes writes one type name and then fails to deserialise as Internal, so this code deliberately builds Internal objects to keep the round trip consistent.

notes.title: Three answers, not one
notes.text: The tuple tells the caller three things: the configuration object, that `embedding_function` must be a separate keyword (0.6.x), and that `hnsw:space` must *also* go into the metadata. A version-adaptive function has to report these differences.

notes.title: The 1.x fallback shape
notes.text: If the typed classes are unavailable, ChromaDB 1.x accepts a plain mapping and carries the embedding function inside it. That is why the caller checks `needs_embedding_function_kwarg` instead of always passing the argument.

notes.title: Idempotent by destruction
notes.text: Drop first, create second. A stale collection from an older JSON file can never mix with fresh embeddings. This is the same habit as `DELETE` + `CREATE` in SQL demos.

notes.title: A bare except, on purpose
notes.text: A brand-new client has nothing to delete and ChromaDB raises. There is no useful recovery, so the error is swallowed. Note this is a bare `except:` - a style warning in most linters; `except Exception:` would be safer because it still lets Ctrl+C through.

notes.title: The second half of the metric fix
notes.text: This single line is what makes `1 - distance` a real cosine similarity on 0.6.x. Remove it and the percentages printed by the CLI become wrong - sometimes negative - while the ranking stays correct. A textbook example of a bug that hides in plain sight.

notes.title: Build the call as a dictionary
notes.text: Because different ChromaDB versions accept different arguments, the call is assembled in a dict and expanded with `**create_kwargs`. Conditional keyword arguments are much clearer this way than two near-identical call sites.

notes.title: One rich document per dish
notes.text: Name, description, ingredients, cuisine, cooking method, taste, health benefits and nutrition all go into the same embedded text. That is why "something sweet and baked with apples" can land on Apple Pie: every field adds signal to one vector.

notes.title: Only append what exists
notes.text: Optional fragments are added only when non-empty, so short records still produce a valid sentence instead of "Taste and features: ."

notes.at: nutrition_text = ', '.join([f"{k}: {v}" for k, v in nutrition.items()])
notes.title: Keep the units in the text
notes.text: Rendering `carbohydrates: 42g` keeps amounts readable both for the embedding model and for a later LLM reading the retrieved chunk. Dropping the units would lose the most useful detail.

notes.title: Collision-safe ids
notes.text: If the JSON repeats a `food_id`, the second copy becomes `7_1`, the third `7_2`. ChromaDB rejects duplicate ids, so one bad row would otherwise kill the whole batch insert.

notes.title: Numeric stays numeric
notes.text: `calories` is stored as a number so `$lte` range filters work. `ingredients` is joined into a string because ChromaDB metadata cannot hold lists. Choosing the right type per field is what makes filtered search possible later.

notes.title: One query, one list-of-lists
notes.text: Even a single query returns `ids[0]`, `distances[0]`, `metadatas[0]`. Forget the outer index and you get a list instead of a value - the most common ChromaDB beginner error.

notes.title: The score contract
notes.text: Cosine distance 0 becomes similarity 1.0. Because the metric is set in both places, this number stays in [0, 1] for sensible matches. It is a ranking signal, not a calibrated probability - do not threshold it blindly.

notes.title: Silent-ish failure
notes.text: The error is printed instead of raised, so the caller sees an empty list. Useful for a CLI, dangerous for a service: a monitoring system would see "zero results", not "broken query".

notes.title: $lte is part of the storage, not the maths
notes.text: The calorie ceiling is applied by the database before ranking, so `n_results` nearest neighbours come from the filtered subset. Filtering after retrieval would give you fewer results than you asked for.

notes.title: One filter, or $and
notes.text: ChromaDB accepts a single condition object, or `{"$and": [...]}` for several. With no filters the clause stays `None`, which degenerates this function into a plain similarity search.

notes.title: 0 silently means "no limit"
notes.text: A truthiness check, not `is not None`. So `max_calories=0` is treated as "no constraint" - a genuine zero-calorie limit cannot be expressed. Documented in the docstring, but still a trap when you reuse this helper.

notes.title: Fixing words before embedding
notes.text: A word-piece tokeniser splits "calroes" into fragments with almost no signal. Repairing a handful of common typos keeps the query on topic without a spell-checker dependency.

notes.title: The regex that reads numbers
notes.text: It matches "under 300", "less than 250 kcal", "max 200 cal" and even "< 150". Two alternatives are captured, which is why the parser later does `group(1) or group(2)`.

notes.title: Facet lookup with a safety net
notes.text: Reading every metadata row once per query is fine for a few hundred dishes; it would not scale to millions. The `or []` handles a `None` return, and the whole block is wrapped so cuisine detection can never break a search.

notes.title: Repair without rewriting
notes.text: Only whole words in the typo table are replaced; everything else - including cuisine names - reaches the embedding model untouched. This keeps user wording intact while fixing the few known holes.

notes.title: Reading whichever group matched
notes.text: Python's `or` returns the first truthy value, so whichever alternative captured the number wins. `int()` then converts the string to a number for the `$lte` filter.

notes.title: Word boundaries and escaping
notes.text: `\b` stops "thai" from matching inside "thailand", and `re.escape` protects cuisine names containing regex characters. The function returns the **canonical** spelling from the database, so the later equality filter matches exactly.

notes.title: No constraint, no extra cost
notes.text: If the parser recognised nothing, the function behaves exactly like plain semantic search. That design keeps ordinary queries fast and makes this wrapper safe to use everywhere.

notes.title: Why 50 candidates, not 5
notes.text: Sorting only the top five by calories would give you the lowest-calorie items *among those five*. A wider pool (default 50) gives the re-ranking something to choose from - but not the whole catalogue, or condiments like Vinegar (3 kcal) would answer every dessert query.

notes.at: if not candidates and constraints["max_calories"] and constraints["cuisine_filter"]:
notes.title: Relax before showing nothing
notes.text: A cuisine plus a calorie ceiling can legitimately match zero dishes. Dropping the numeric cap is friendlier than an empty screen, and the calorie sorting below still helps. Every fallback like this should be deliberate and documented - this one is.

notes.title: Stable sort keeps relevance ties
notes.text: Python's sort is stable, so two dishes with the same calories keep their semantic order. The `or 0` guards against a `None` calorie value sneaking in.

notes.title: Slice after sorting
notes.text: Sort the whole pool, then keep the first five. Slicing first and sorting second would return the five most similar dishes sorted among themselves - the wrong answer to "lowest calories".

Food_Recommender/interactive_search.py.purpose: The conversation layer: load the catalogue, build the Chroma collection, then run a command-line chatbot that searches, shows match percentages, suggests related searches and remembers what you typed.
Food_Recommender/interactive_search.py.run: python interactive_search.py   (needs FoodDataSet.json in the same folder)

sections.title: Wildcard import and module-level state
sections.why: One line brings in every helper, and two module variables remember the catalogue and the search history for the whole session.

sections.title: main() - load, index, chat
sections.why: Three steps and one try/except. If the catalogue or the collection fails, the user sees one clear message instead of a traceback.

sections.title: The chat loop
sections.why: A `while True` loop with explicit commands, empty-input handling and Ctrl+C support. This is the template for every CLI bot in the repo.

sections.title: Help and history
sections.why: Two tiny functions that make an otherwise bare prompt feel like a product.

sections.title: handle_food_search() - the actual query
sections.why: Calls the calorie-aware search, prints each result with a percentage, and then suggests follow-up searches.

sections.title: Suggesting follow-up searches
sections.why: Turns the result set into new query ideas - a cheap way to help a user who does not know what to type.

notes.title: Convenient and risky
notes.text: `import *` pulls in every public name, including `json`, `re` and `np` that the module happens to import. It saves typing in a demo, but in a real project it hides where a name came from and makes refactoring painful. Prefer explicit imports.

notes.title: Module-level mutable state
notes.text: Both lists live at module scope so several functions can share them without passing arguments. Handy here; in larger programs it is the usual source of "why is my data from the previous run?" bugs.

notes.title: The global statement
notes.text: Without `global`, the assignments below would create *local* variables and the rest of the module would keep seeing empty lists. Python requires this declaration to mutate a module-level name inside a function.

notes.title: Relative path, so run it from this folder
notes.text: `./FoodDataSet.json` is relative to the **current working directory**, not to this file. Run the script from another folder and loading fails with a friendly `Error loading food data` message.

notes.title: Create, then populate
notes.text: The collection starts empty. `populate_similarity_collection` embeds and inserts. Forget that second call and every search returns nothing - a very common bug when copying a ChromaDB example.

notes.title: One failure point in main
notes.text: Setup errors - file missing, Chroma version mismatch, model download failure - all surface here with a printed reason. The CLI never starts if setup is broken, which is clearer than failing on the first query.

notes.title: strip() before comparing
notes.text: Trailing spaces are invisible but break equality checks: `"quit "` is not `"quit"`. Stripping first means a stray space does not silently turn a command into a search.

notes.title: Handle the empty Enter key
notes.text: Pressing Enter with no text is the most common user action. Printing a hint and `continue`-ing keeps the loop alive instead of searching for an empty string.

notes.title: Commands before search
notes.text: Command matching happens before the search branch, so the word "quit" can never be treated as a food query. Order of checks is logic, not style.

notes.title: Ctrl+C should look intentional
notes.text: Without this, Ctrl+C dumps a KeyboardInterrupt traceback. Catching it and saying goodbye is the difference between "the program crashed" and "I stopped it".

notes.title: The loop survives one bad query
notes.text: An unexpected error prints and the loop continues. Note that this also hides programming mistakes, so during development it is worth temporarily re-raising.

notes.title: Recorded before searching
notes.text: The query is saved even when the search fails or returns nothing - which is exactly what you want when reviewing what users actually asked.

notes.title: The smart wrapper, not plain search
notes.text: This one call handles typos, cuisine words and calorie intent. The three-line comment above explains when it behaves like a plain semantic search - worth preserving in any rewrite.

notes.title: A percentage that can be negative
notes.text: The value is a cosine similarity in [-1, 1], so an unrelated dish can print as a negative percentage. It looks wrong to users. Clamp with `max(0, score)` or show the raw score instead.

notes.title: enumerate with start=1
notes.text: `enumerate(results, 1)` numbers the list from 1 for humans while keeping Python's 0-based indexing internal. No more `i + 1` sprinkled through the print statements.

notes.title: Formatting floats for humans
notes.text: `:.1f` prints one decimal place, so 72.4318 becomes 72.4%. Consistent formatting makes a column of results scannable.

notes.at: cuisines = list(set([r['cuisine_type'] for r in results]))
notes.title: Deduplicate with a set
notes.text: Five results often share one cuisine. A set removes duplicates, and `list(...)` converts it back for slicing. Because sets are unordered, the three suggestions shown can vary between runs.

notes.at: avg_calories = sum([r['food_calories_per_serving'] for r in results]) / len(results)
notes.title: Divide safely
notes.text: This line runs only after the `if not results: return` guard above, so `len(results)` is never zero. Removing that guard would produce a ZeroDivisionError.

notes.title: Slicing the tail
notes.text: `[-10:]` shows the last ten searches, newest last. Negative slicing is safe even when there are fewer than ten entries.

notes.title: Guard, so importing stays quiet
notes.text: This module is imported by nobody, but the guard is still correct: importing it must not start an interactive input loop.

Food_Recommender/FoodDataSet.json.purpose: The catalogue: a JSON array of dish objects. One record is shown here (lines 1-40 of 5,081) because every record has the same shape, and that shape is what the Python code assumes.

sections.title: One complete dish record
sections.why: Read the keys carefully - each one has a matching line of Python that either embeds it, stores it as metadata, or filters on it.

notes.title: An array of objects
notes.text: The outer `[` makes this a JSON list, which is why `json.load` returns a Python list and `load_food_data` can loop over it directly.

notes.title: Integer here, string later
notes.text: JSON has no separate integer-string distinction beyond the quotes. `load_food_data` converts this to `"1"` because ChromaDB ids must be strings.

notes.title: A number, not text
notes.text: Because this is numeric, the `$lte` filter and the ascending sort both work. If it were `"320"`, comparisons would be string-based and 90 would sort after 320.

notes.title: Nested object, flattened for embedding
notes.text: The embedder needs text, not a dict. `populate_similarity_collection` renders this as `carbohydrates: 42g, protein: 2g, fat: 16g` inside the document string.

notes.title: A list must become a string
notes.text: ChromaDB metadata cannot store lists, so ingredients are joined with commas for metadata and also joined inside the embedded text. The original list is still available in the loaded Python object.

notes.title: The source of taste_profile
notes.text: These five sub-fields (taste, texture, appearance, preparation, serving type) are flattened by `load_food_data` into `taste_profile`, which then appears in both the embedding text and the metadata.

notes.title: The value that filters compare exactly
notes.text: The cuisine filter is an exact string match, so `"American"` and `"american"` are different values. That is why `parse_search_constraints` returns the canonical spelling read from the database instead of the user's typing.
